title: FSB puts stablecoins and AI at the centre of G20 supervisory priorities
summary: The FSB's October 2026 letter to G20 finance ministers elevates stablecoins and AI to active supervisory priorities, not future-watch items. Alex and Jordan disagree on what that means for AML controls today, plus two overdue Hong Kong obligations that cannot wait.
script:
ALEX: Andrew Bailey sent a letter to G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors yesterday, ahead of their Bangkok meeting, and I want to be precise about what changed. This is not a watching brief. The Financial Stability Board has moved its stablecoin monitoring framework from preparatory to active. That is a material shift in supervisory posture, and I think compliance teams are underweighting it.

JORDAN: I will push back on that framing slightly. The FSB publishing sound practices on artificial intelligence and renewing its stablecoin monitoring framework in the same letter is a lot of signals firing at once. And in my experience, when a global standard-setter fires two signals simultaneously, practitioners end up responding to neither with any depth. So before we get into what changed, I want to name that risk. This is AML Agents Briefing for Tuesday the thirteenth of October.

ALEX: That is a fair point, and I think it actually reinforces why the stablecoin piece deserves the sharper focus today. The AI sound practices are important, but the stablecoin monitoring shift has a more immediate read-across to existing AML and counter-financing of terrorism controls. Bailey's letter explicitly frames cross-border vulnerability in stablecoin arrangements as a systemic concern, not just a crypto-sector concern. That matters for every correspondent bank and every payment institution in this region that is touching dollar-denominated stablecoin flows.

JORDAN: Right, and here is where I would sharpen the point further. The FSB note to G20 on global stablecoin arrangements confirms that cross-border monitoring is now an active supervisory priority. What that means operationally is that your transaction monitoring rules designed around traditional wire flows are probably not calibrated for stablecoin settlement patterns. The velocity is different. The counterparty opacity is different. And if your regulator in Singapore or Hong Kong or Australia comes in and asks how you monitor cross-border stablecoin exposure, answering "we treat it like a wire transfer" is not going to land well anymore.

ALEX: I think that is exactly the right read on the Singapore and Hong Kong positions. I am slightly less convinced it has immediate bite in Australia, where AUSTRAC's tranche-two reforms are still the dominant operational priority for most firms. The FSB framework creates the normative pressure, but the domestic supervisory translation takes time.

JORDAN: I hear you, but I would not give Australian compliance teams that much comfort. AUSTRAC has been explicit that designated non-financial businesses and professions onboarding under the expanded regime need to think about digital-asset exposure from day one. If the FSB is signalling to central banks that stablecoin monitoring needs to be active now, the expectation is going to flow downstream faster than people assume. I have sat in enough AUSTRAC consultation rooms to know they read FSB outputs very carefully.

ALEX: Fair enough. So let's get to the action item here, because I think the practical question is: what do you actually do with this today?

JORDAN: If you are a Money Laundering Reporting Officer at a payment institution, a virtual asset service provider, or frankly any bank with a digital-assets desk, the concrete step is to pull your transaction monitoring coverage matrix this week and map it against stablecoin typologies specifically. Not generic crypto. Stablecoin. Look at cross-border corridors first, because that is where the FSB's monitoring focus lands. If you have gaps in inbound and outbound flow visibility, your know-your-transaction vendor integration needs to be on the agenda before your next risk committee meeting. And document that review. When your supervisor asks, you want to show the date you responded to the FSB signal, not the date your supervisor raised it with you.

ALEX: On the AI sound practices piece, I will note it briefly. The FSB has finalised those practices, and Bailey's framing makes clear that AI governance in financial institutions is now a Board-level expectation, not a future concern. For financial crime compliance, the read-across is that if your firm is using AI in transaction monitoring, adverse-media screening, or customer risk scoring, you need a governance wrapper around it that can withstand a supervisory examination. That means model risk management, explainability, and bias testing as standing disciplines, not one-off exercises.

JORDAN: Agreed, and I will add: if your Chief Risk Officer is not already owning the AI governance piece alongside your Chief Compliance Officer, that is a gap worth surfacing. The FSB is framing this as a systemic risk issue, which means it will travel up the regulatory chain quickly.

ALEX: Moving on, and I want to spend a moment on Hong Kong because there are two obligations on the board that deserve attention from any listener with HKMA-supervised AI responsibilities.

JORDAN: The first is the HKMA Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism Guideline, specifically paragraph 11, which requires an annual self-assessment return covering customer due diligence, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious transaction reporting filing, training, governance, and independent audit. The submission deadline was September 30. If you have not submitted, that is overdue now.

ALEX: And the second is more uncomfortable. The HKMA issued a Q4 2025 thematic review of suspicious transaction report narrative quality across HKMA-supervised authorised institutions. Deficiency letters went to roughly twenty-five percent of the authorised institution population. Closure of those findings is the current high-priority obligation. If your institution received one of those letters and the remediation plan is not formally closed, that needs to be escalating to your senior management this week, not sitting in a working-level tracker.

JORDAN: The thing I would add here is that STR narrative quality is a recurring HKMA examination theme. If you received a deficiency letter, the response the HKMA is looking for is not just a corrected template. They want to see training records, updated typology guidance for your analysts, and ideally a re-review sample showing improvement. That is the kind of evidence pack that closes a thematic finding cleanly.

ALEX: And for Singapore listeners, the MAS Notice 626 paragraph 6 quarterly suspicious transaction report governance review is also on the active obligations list. Completeness, timeliness, escalation effectiveness, and STRO acknowledgement reconciliation. If that review is not completed for the most recent quarter, it needs to be scheduled this week.

JORDAN: Before we close, I want to name the Vietnam item briefly. The World Bank Group assessment referencing ASIFMA's advocacy on Vietnam's anticipated reclassification from frontier to emerging-market status is more than a capital-markets story. For compliance officers at international broker-dealers and custodians, onboarding a new wave of Vietnamese institutional counterparties means your customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence frameworks need to be reviewed for fit. Vietnam remains on the Financial Action Task Force grey list as of this recording. Emerging-market reclassification does not change that. Make sure your front-line onboarding teams understand the distinction before the volume arrives.

ALEX: That is the right note to end on. The week ahead has the G20 Bangkok meeting as the backdrop, so expect further signalling on stablecoins and non-bank financial intermediation. Watch for any joint communique language on supervisory expectations, because that is how FSB priorities become domestic regulatory priorities in this region.

JORDAN: If your stablecoin monitoring coverage, your HKMA self-assessment, or your STR remediation pack felt uncomfortably vague while you were listening to this, that is your action list for the rest of the week. The full obligation register and source links are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. See you tomorrow.
